statement:
Imagine that in a rain storm, all the raindrops fall straight down with constant velocity $$v_{\rm rain}$$

You need to go from building A to building B during the rain storm, but you don't have an umbrella. You want to know whether you should walk or run, assuming you want to minimize the amount of rain that hits you as you go from building to building. (Assume that walking and running are the same except for how fast you go, so don't worry about limbs flailing around.) Your speed as you go from building to building is $$v_{\rm you}.$$

Which **one** of the following scenarios is equivalent to this setup? Use Galilean relativity for this question.

Answer by submitting a single letter.

**a**

You are stationary, the rain still falls vertically at speed $$v_{\rm rain},$$ the buildings and ground move to the left at speed $$v_{\rm you}.$$

**b**

You are stationary, the rain falls down and to the left at speed $$\sqrt{v_{\rm rain}^2 + v_{\rm you}^2},$$ and the buildings and ground move left at speed $$v_{\rm you}.$$

**c**

The rain is stationary, the buildings and ground are stationary, and you move right at speed $$v_{\rm you}.$$

**d**

You are stationary, the buildings and ground move left at speed $$v_{\rm you},$$ and the rain moves purely left at speed $$v_{\rm you}.$$

If the wind is blowing at a steady speed (the same wind speed everywhere), and the wind is horizontal, what happens to the speed of sound in the air (measured relative to the Earth)?

**b**

desc: In a famous shot from the movie __Hugo__, a train appears to pull through a station while an inspector, stuck to one of its doors, is dragged along. To the viewer, the train seems to move to the right past the camera, so that by the end of the shot the inspector and the door…
statement:
In a famous shot from the movie __Hugo__, a train appears to pull through a station while an inspector, stuck to one of its doors, is dragged along. To the viewer, the train seems to move to the right past the camera, so that by the end of the shot the inspector and the door he's stuck on are __to the right of the camera__. Here is the shot:

Surprise: the film crew would say the train was __not__ moving when this was filmed. They built the station platform as a giant movable rig, mounted the camera on it, and dragged the platform and camera to one side while leaving the train alone. Here is a behind-the-scenes photo:

__(a)__ Which direction did the crew drag the platform and camera — to the left or to the right?

__(b)__ Explain why the resulting footage looks exactly the same as footage of a genuinely moving train would. (Think about where everything ends up __relative to the camera__.)

__(c)__ If you had been standing on the ground watching the filming in real life, which would you say was "really" moving — the train or the platform? Why does the answer feel different for someone watching the finished movie? Use the idea of a __reference frame__ — a choice of object that we treat as stationary — in your answer. (Most of us habitually use the __rest frame of the ground__, the frame in which the ground is stationary. If you've ever been on a train that starts moving forward and briefly felt that the buildings outside were drifting backwards, you've felt your mind switch reference frames.)

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: Galileo's Ship and the Principle of Relativity — Long before Einstein, Galileo wanted to convince people that…
desc: Long before Einstein, Galileo wanted to convince people that the Earth could move around the Sun without anyone on Earth feeling the motion. He asked people to imagine a ship moving __perfectly smoothly__ through the ocean: always the same speed and the same direction, with no…
statement:
Long before Einstein, Galileo wanted to convince people that the Earth could move around the Sun without anyone on Earth feeling the motion. He asked people to imagine a ship moving __perfectly smoothly__ through the ocean: always the same speed and the same direction, with no waves or rocking. (Speed and direction together are called __velocity__, so the ship moves with constant velocity.) Alex rides inside the ship, and Lizzie watches from an island; she can see inside the ship. The picture shows the scene in Lizzie's reference frame, with the ship sailing to the right.

__(a)__ Alex draws a line on the floor (line 1), stands on it, and jumps toward the front of the ship — the same direction the ship is moving. He draws line 2 where he lands. Then he stands on line 2 and jumps back the same way, this time jumping __opposite__ to the ship's motion. Where does he land: right at line 1, short of line 1, or past line 1?

__(b)__ Galileo claimed much more than this: __any__ experiment conducted inside the smoothly moving ship — shining lasers around, measuring the speed of sound, even running a particle accelerator — gives exactly the same result as it would on a stationary ship. This is the __principle of relativity__. Now suppose the ship suddenly slams into an island. Alex can certainly tell that happened! Why doesn't this violate the principle of relativity? Your answer should use the term __inertial reference frame__: a reference frame moving with constant velocity.

__(c)__ A star far away is stationary in Lizzie's frame. What is the star doing in Alex's frame? Galileo invented a fictional critic, Simplicio, who objects: "The star is either moving or it is not. Either way, one of Lizzie or Alex has to be wrong. Therefore, not all reference frames are equivalent." Refute Simplicio. This analogy may help: Alex and Lizzie stand facing each other from across a road, with their friend Grogg far down the road. Alex says "Grogg is to my left"; Lizzie says "Grogg is to my right." Who is correct?

__(d)__ Even though Alex and Lizzie disagree about the star's velocity, name two things about the situation that they do agree on.

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: The Rule for Transforming Reference Frames — Alex, Lizzie, and Grogg each fly a small spaceship in deep…
desc: Alex, Lizzie, and Grogg each fly a small spaceship in deep space, all moving along the same line. The picture below shows the situation in one particular reference frame: Alex is stationary, Lizzie moves to the right at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and Grogg moves to the right at…
statement:
Alex, Lizzie, and Grogg each fly a small spaceship in deep space, all moving along the same line. The picture below shows the situation in one particular reference frame: Alex is stationary, Lizzie moves to the right at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and Grogg moves to the right at $$10\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Switching from one reference frame to another is called __transforming__ between frames; this problem develops the precise rule for doing it.

__(a)__ Whose reference frame is the picture drawn from? How can you tell?

__(b)__ Now transform to Lizzie's frame, in which Lizzie is stationary. What is Alex doing in this frame?

__(c)__ In Galilean relativity, we assume that distances and times are the same in all reference frames. Consider the distance from Lizzie to Grogg. In the frame shown, how fast does that distance grow? Assuming it grows at the same rate in every frame, find Grogg's velocity (speed and direction) in Lizzie's frame.

__(d)__ Based on your answers, state a short, general rule for what we do to each object's velocity when transforming between inertial frames. What velocity did we add to every object to go from Alex's frame to Lizzie's frame? What velocity would we add to transform back?

__(e)__ Is there a rule that some particular object must be stationary in the new frame? For example, would it be legitimate to transform by adding $$2\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ to the right — or even some velocity pointing straight up — to every object?

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: Events, Invariants, and Measuring a Moving Pencil — An __event__ is a specific point in space and time. A…
desc: An __event__ is a specific point in space and time. A handclap marks an event: it happens at a definite place and at a definite moment. A quantity that is the same in all reference frames is called __invariant__. In Galilean relativity, two basic assumptions are that the length…
statement:
An __event__ is a specific point in space and time. A handclap marks an event: it happens at a definite place and at a definite moment. A quantity that is the same in all reference frames is called __invariant__. In Galilean relativity, two basic assumptions are that the length of an object is invariant and that the time between two events is invariant. In this problem, Alex rides a ship moving steadily past Lizzie's island, and she can see inside the ship.

__(a)__ Alex drops his mug, and Lizzie, watching from her island, calls out "Oh no!" Is "Alex drops his mug and Lizzie calls out" a single event? Separately: is "the mug falls and shatters when it hits the deck" a single event?

__(b)__ Alex claps his hands, waits a moment, and claps again. Each clap is an event. In whose reference frame is the __distance__ between the two handclap events zero — Alex's, Lizzie's, both, or neither? What does this tell you about whether the distance between a pair of events is invariant, even in Galilean relativity?

__(c)__ Here is how we measure a pencil: line up the tip of the pencil with the $$0\;\mathrm{cm}$$ mark on a ruler (call this event 1), then read the ruler marking at the back of the pencil — say it reads $$11\;\mathrm{cm}$$ (event 2).

Now suppose the pencil happens to be sliding to the right relative to the ruler, toward higher markings, and event 2 happens a short time after event 1. Will the measured length be too big, too small, or correct? In general, what must be true of events 1 and 2 to measure a moving object's length correctly?

__(d)__ Simplicio argues: "Let event 1 be Alex jumping from line 1 on the ship's floor, and event 2 be Alex landing on line 2. The distance between the lines is invariant — it's just the length of a stretch of floor. Therefore the distance between the two events is invariant too!" Find Simplicio's mistake.

__(b)__ Having settled the outcome in the cart's frame, switch back to the ground frame and describe the path of the ball there. The third clip shows the experiment done in real life.

__(c)__ After the frame switch, is scenario 2 __exactly__ the same situation as scenario 1? Identify at least one physical difference, and explain why this calls for care when using the principle of relativity — without making the principle itself only approximately true.

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: Treadmill Bicycles, Steady Elevators, and Tailwinds — Each part of this problem is an everyday puzzle that…
desc: Each part of this problem is an everyday puzzle that becomes simple in the right reference frame. Throughout, use Galilean relativity: to transform frames, add the same velocity to every object, and remember that experiments come out the same in all inertial (constant-velocity)…
statement:
Each part of this problem is an everyday puzzle that becomes simple in the right reference frame. Throughout, use Galilean relativity: to transform frames, add the same velocity to every object, and remember that experiments come out the same in all inertial (constant-velocity) frames.

__(a)__ Simplicio says, "You can't balance on a bicycle when stationary — you have to ride forward to stay balanced. This means you can't ride a bicycle on a treadmill, because the bike wouldn't be going anywhere and would fall over." Decide whether he is right. Analyze the situation from the reference frame in which the __top of the treadmill belt__ is stationary: what are the treadmill body, the gym, and the rider doing in that frame, and does the event "rider falls over" occur? (A professional cyclist demonstrates below. Don't try it — drifting an inch to either side means crashing.)

__(b)__ You stand on a scale inside an elevator. Apart from brief moments at the beginning and end of the ride, the elevator moves up or down at constant speed as seen from the ground. Is the scale reading higher when the elevator moves up at constant speed, when it moves down at constant speed, or is it the same? When during the ride __does__ the reading change?

__(c)__ You hang a weight from a rubber band and hold the other end in your hand. You can hold the weight steady, lift it at a steady rate, or lower it at a steady rate. Assuming the band isn't oscillating, during which of these is the rubber band most stretched?

__(d)__ City A lies $$360\;\mathrm{km}$$ west of city B. When there is no wind, an airplane can fly from A to B and back in $$2.0\;\mathrm{hr}.$$ Now a steady wind blows from west to east at $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ (i) Using the reference frame of the air, justify the standard assumption that a $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ tailwind makes the plane move $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ faster over the ground and a headwind $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ slower. (ii) Find the round-trip time with the wind blowing. (iii) A bicyclist with a $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ tailwind does __not__ speed up by $$20\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ — the wind just flows around them, pushing them forward only a little. Why does the frame argument work for the plane but fail for the bicycle?

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: Einstein's Puzzle and the Invariant Speed of Light — Einstein invented special relativity while puzzling over…
desc: Einstein invented special relativity while puzzling over electricity and magnetism. Imagine a loop of wire with a light bulb in it. If you move a magnet toward the loop, the magnet makes electrons flow around the loop, and the bulb lights up: __(a)__ Suppose instead you hold the…
statement:
Einstein invented special relativity while puzzling over electricity and magnetism. Imagine a loop of wire with a light bulb in it. If you move a magnet toward the loop, the magnet makes electrons flow around the loop, and the bulb lights up:

__(a)__ Suppose instead you hold the magnet steady and move the __loop__ toward it at the same relative speed (shown below). Using only the principle of relativity — no electromagnetic theory — what must happen to the bulb, and why? (What puzzled Einstein: physicists of his day agreed on the outcome, but explained the two cases by entirely different mechanisms — a magnetic field pushing the electrons of the moving loop in one case, and a newly created electric field pushing them in the other. He wanted one unified picture.)

__(b)__ James Clerk Maxwell's theory of electromagnetism contains a fixed speed at which light (electromagnetic radiation) travels: $$c = 299{,}792{,}458\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Since the laws of physics should be the same in all inertial frames, Einstein postulated that $$c$$ is __invariant__ — the same in every frame. Now: Lizzie, in a spaceship, sees a flash of light go by to the right at speed $$c.$$ She also sees Alex in his ship chasing the flash at speed $$c/10.$$ What is the speed of the flash in Alex's frame (i) according to the Galilean transformation rule, and (ii) according to Einstein's postulate? Which rule does the postulate break?

__(c)__ Here is a proposed __proof__ of the Galilean velocity-transformation rule. Alex marks a start line and a finish line in deep space, $$20\;\mathrm{m}$$ apart (in his frame). Grogg flies from start to finish in $$2\;\mathrm{s}$$ (in Alex's frame), so his speed in Alex's frame is $$v_{G;A}=\dfrac{20\;\mathrm{m}}{2\;\mathrm{s}}=10\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Lizzie starts alongside Grogg but takes $$5\;\mathrm{s},$$ so $$v_{L;A}=4\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

The proof runs: let event 1 be Grogg crossing the start line and event 2 be Grogg crossing the finish line, and view them from Lizzie's frame. The time between the events is $$2\;\mathrm{s}$$ there too. In Lizzie's frame the finish line approaches Grogg at $$4\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ so during those $$2\;\mathrm{s}$$ it moves $$8\;\mathrm{m}$$ toward him, and Grogg himself only travels $$20\;\mathrm{m}-8\;\mathrm{m}=12\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Therefore his speed in Lizzie's frame is $$\dfrac{12\;\mathrm{m}}{2\;\mathrm{s}}=6\;\mathrm{m/s}=10\;\mathrm{m/s}-4\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ which is the Galilean rule. Since Einstein's postulate says the rule fails for light, some assumption in this proof must be wrong. Identify the assumptions the proof quietly makes.
tags: principle of relativity, speed of light, and time dilation

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: The Light Clock and Time Dilation — A __thought experiment__ is an experiment we run in our minds. Here is…
desc: A __thought experiment__ is an experiment we run in our minds. Here is the most famous one in relativity. Two mirrors face each other, and a flash of light bounces back and forth between them — a __light clock__. Say a round trip takes exactly one second, and a small clock face…
statement:
A __thought experiment__ is an experiment we run in our minds. Here is the most famous one in relativity. Two mirrors face each other, and a flash of light bounces back and forth between them — a __light clock__. Say a round trip takes exactly one second, and a small clock face ticks forward one second every time the flash returns to the bottom mirror. Alex and Lizzie carry identical light clocks; Lizzie's spaceship moves to the right at speed $$v$$ relative to Alex. Use two facts: light moves at the invariant speed $$c$$ in every inertial frame (Einstein's postulate), and __which events occur__ is invariant — if an event happens in one frame, it happens in every frame.

__(a)__ In Lizzie's own frame, the flash in her clock travels straight up and down, striking the center of each mirror with every bounce. Each strike is an event. Use the invariance of events to determine what the flash's path in Lizzie's clock looks like in __Alex's__ frame.

__(b)__ In Alex's frame, does the light in Lizzie's clock travel a longer, shorter, or equal distance per tick compared with the light in his own clock? Given that all light moves at the same speed $$c,$$ does Lizzie's clock tick more often, less often, or just as often as Alex's, in Alex's frame?

__(c)__ There are many other kinds of clocks: mechanical (wound springs drive the ticking), quartz (counts crystal vibrations), atomic (measures the frequency of light from certain atoms), and nuclear-decay clocks (measure radiation rates). Suppose Lizzie carries one of each, all in the same place, and in her frame they all tick together with her light clock. Use the invariance of events to argue that, in Alex's frame, __every one__ of these clocks runs slow by the same factor as the light clock. What does that suggest about time itself in Lizzie's ship, as viewed by Alex?

__(d)__ What does Lizzie herself experience inside her ship — slow motion, fast forward, or everything normal? And what does Lizzie observe about __Alex's__ light clock?

__(e)__ Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere create particles called __muons__, which shoot toward the ground at nearly the speed of light. A muon at rest lasts only about $$0.000002\;\mathrm{s}$$ before decaying. Multiply that lifetime by the speed of light (round it to $$300{,}000{,}000\;\mathrm{m/s}$$) to find how far a muon could travel if its lifetime weren't affected by motion. The muons are created many kilometers up, yet detectors on the surface of the Earth routinely catch them. Explain how this confirms time dilation.

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: The Lorentz Factor — Moving clocks run slow — but by how much? The factor by which a moving clock runs slow…
desc: Moving clocks run slow — but by how much? The factor by which a moving clock runs slow is called the __Lorentz factor__, written $$\gamma$$ (the Greek letter gamma). If a moving clock runs at half speed, $$\gamma=2$$; at one-third speed, $$\gamma=3.$$ The factor depends on the…
statement:
Moving clocks run slow — but by how much? The factor by which a moving clock runs slow is called the __Lorentz factor__, written $$\gamma$$ (the Greek letter gamma). If a moving clock runs at half speed, $$\gamma=2$$; at one-third speed, $$\gamma=3.$$ The factor depends on the clock's speed $$v,$$ so we write it as the function $$\gamma(v).$$ (Hendrik Lorentz found this factor in 1892, thirteen years before Einstein's theory — no scientific idea pops up out of nowhere.) Work in Alex's frame, where Lizzie's light clock — a flash bouncing between two mirrors — slides to the right at speed $$v,$$ its flash tracing a zigzag at speed $$c.$$

__(a)__ Before any algebra, pin down the shape of the graph of $$\gamma(v).$$ What should $$\gamma(0)$$ be, given that we notice no time dilation in everyday life? Should $$\gamma$$ increase or decrease as $$v$$ grows? And by imagining the zigzag when Lizzie moves at, say, $$0.99999c$$ — light spending almost all its speed just keeping up with the clock — describe what $$\gamma$$ does as $$v$$ approaches $$c.$$

__(b)__ Let $$u$$ be the __vertical__ part of the flash's velocity in Alex's frame — the part that actually carries light between the mirrors and makes the clock tick. Explain why $$\gamma=\dfrac{c}{u}.$$ (For instance, what would $$\gamma$$ be if $$u=0.1c?$$)

__(c)__ The flash's velocity has horizontal part $$v$$ (it must keep up with the clock) and vertical part $$u,$$ while its total speed is $$c.$$ These form a right triangle with hypotenuse $$c$$:

Use the Pythagorean theorem to find $$u$$ in terms of $$v$$ and $$c,$$ and derive the formula for $$\gamma(v).$$

__(d)__ Check your formula at $$v=0$$ and as $$v\to c$$ against your answers in part (a). What does the formula suggest would happen to Lizzie's time if she moved at exactly $$c$$ — or faster?

__(e)__ How fast must Lizzie fly, in Alex's frame, so that her clock runs at $$\dfrac12$$ normal speed according to Alex?

__(f)__ Estimate how much time your wristwatch loses when you fly across the United States: a jet flies at roughly $$v\approx300\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ — about one-millionth of the speed of light — and the trip takes about five hours. At this speed the Lorentz factor works out to $$\gamma\approx1+5\times10^{-13},$$ a number just barely bigger than one. About how much time does the watch lose? Could any clock detect such a shift?

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: Grogg's One-Light-Year Trip — Alex and Lizzie float at rest relative to each other in deep space, one __light…
desc: Alex and Lizzie float at rest relative to each other in deep space, one __light year__ apart. A light year ($$\mathrm{ly}$$) is a __distance__, not a time: the distance light travels in one year. Since $$c=299{,}792{,}458\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and one year is…
statement:
Alex and Lizzie float at rest relative to each other in deep space, one __light year__ apart. A light year ($$\mathrm{ly}$$) is a __distance__, not a time: the distance light travels in one year. Since $$c=299{,}792{,}458\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and one year is $$31{,}557{,}600\;\mathrm{s},$$ we have $$1\;\mathrm{ly}=c\cdot(1\;\mathrm{year})\approx9.46\times10^{15}\;\mathrm{m}$$ — about $$5.88$$ trillion miles. (For scale: the nearest stars beyond the Sun are about $$4\;\mathrm{ly}$$ away, and our galaxy is about $$50{,}000\;\mathrm{ly}$$ across.) Grogg flies past Alex at constant speed, headed straight for Lizzie, and starts a stopwatch just as he passes Alex. Just as he reaches Lizzie, his stopwatch reads exactly one year. Recall the Lorentz factor $$\gamma(v)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}.$$

__(a)__ Warm-up: if a star one million light years away (in our frame) exploded, how long would it be before we could possibly know about it?

__(b)__ If you didn't know about special relativity — so that one year on Grogg's stopwatch meant one year for everyone — how fast would Grogg have to travel to cover one light year in that time? Explain why, with time dilation, Grogg doesn't actually need to go that fast. While Grogg's stopwatch advances by one year, does more or less than one year pass for Alex and Lizzie?

__(c)__ Let $$v$$ be Grogg's speed in Alex and Lizzie's frame. Write the trip time in their frame, $$t_{LA},$$ in terms of $$v$$; then write the time $$t_G$$ that elapses on Grogg's stopwatch, using time dilation. Set $$t_G$$ equal to one year and solve for $$v.$$ (The identity $$1\;\mathrm{ly}=c\cdot(1\;\mathrm{year})$$ will simplify things.)

__(d)__ Sanity check: at $$v=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}c\approx0.87c,$$ the Lorentz factor is exactly $$\gamma=2.$$ If Grogg made the same one-light-year trip at $$0.87c,$$ how much time would pass on his stopwatch? Is that consistent with your answer to part (c)?
tags: principle of relativity, speed of light, and time dilation

lesson: REL01: Principle of Relativity, Speed of Light, and Time Dilation
label: REL01
name: Whose Clock Is Really Slow? — Lizzie flies past Alex in a very close flyby at constant velocity, fast enough…
desc: Lizzie flies past Alex in a very close flyby at constant velocity, fast enough that $$\gamma=3.$$ In Alex's frame, Lizzie's clock runs at one-third speed. But in Lizzie's frame, __Alex__ is the one moving, so his clock runs at one-third speed. Each says the other's clock is…
statement:
Lizzie flies past Alex in a very close flyby at constant velocity, fast enough that $$\gamma=3.$$ In Alex's frame, Lizzie's clock runs at one-third speed. But in Lizzie's frame, __Alex__ is the one moving, so his clock runs at one-third speed. Each says the other's clock is slow! Many people object that this is a flat contradiction: even if something slowed both clocks down, they'd merely stay in sync — surely they can't each run slower than the other. This problem pins down why there is no contradiction. Recall: an __event__ is a single point in space and time; __which events occur__ is invariant (the same in all frames); but in special relativity, neither the time between events nor whether two events are __simultaneous__ (happen at the same time) is invariant.

__(a)__ Is "Lizzie passes by Alex" technically an event, given our definition? Why can we nevertheless idealize it as one? At the flyby, both reset their clocks to read zero; since this happens at (essentially) one event, we can name it $$L_0=A_0.$$

__(b)__ Alex says: "Since $$\gamma=3,$$ Lizzie's first tick happens just as my clock makes its third tick." Lizzie replies: "In my frame, my first tick happens when your clock is only one-third of the way through its first tick!" Let $$L_1$$ be the event "Lizzie's clock ticks for the first time" and $$A_3$$ the event "Alex's clock ticks for the third time." Does Lizzie agree that both $$L_1$$ and $$A_3$$ occur? Explain how Alex's and Lizzie's statements can both be correct without different events happening in different frames — and identify exactly which assumption a skeptic must give up.

__(c)__ Alex proposes a test: "We'll do the flyby and reset our clocks. Then, after one hour, we'll both freeze. Then we'll be in the same reference frame and can compare clocks." Find at least two problems with this instruction as stated. Suppose instead that after one hour __on her own clock__, Lizzie fires her engines until she is at rest relative to Alex, and they then compare clocks; her clock will read behind his. Does this prove that her clock was "really" the slow one all along?

__(d)__ Another scheme: "As soon as we are one light year apart, we will both set our clocks to zero. Then when we pass each other, whoever's clock is behind is the one really experiencing time dilation." What goes wrong with this plan?

__(e)__ Before Einstein, many scientists believed in the "aether" — a fluid filling the universe that could physically push on moving objects, shortening them and slowing their clocks like thick honey. Is there any mechanism of this sort slowing the hands of Lizzie's clock in special relativity? Use the invariance of which-events-occur to answer.

name: A train sits on train tracks. The wheels of the train are a distance $$\ell$$ apart, and…

statement:
A train sits on train tracks. The wheels of the train are a distance $$\ell$$ apart, and the tracks are also a distance $$\ell$$ apart so that the train sits on the tracks.

When the train moves at $$v \approx 0.87 c,$$ the Lorentz factor $$\gamma = 2.$$

label: REL02
name: The Muon Paradox, From the Muon's Point of View — Muons are subatomic particles created when cosmic rays…
desc: Muons are subatomic particles created when cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere, about $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground. A muon lives only about $$0.000002\;\mathrm{s}$$ before decaying, yet muons are routinely detected at Earth's surface. Analyzed from the ground…
statement:
Muons are subatomic particles created when cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere, about $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground. A muon lives only about $$0.000002\;\mathrm{s}$$ before decaying, yet muons are routinely detected at Earth's surface. Analyzed from the ground, the resolution is __time dilation__: the muon travels at nearly the speed of light $$c = 3\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ so its internal clock runs slowly by the Lorentz factor $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}},$$ stretching its lifetime as measured on Earth. In this problem, analyze the same trip from the __muon's own reference frame__ instead.

__(a)__ In the muon's own reference frame, what is the muon's velocity? What are the Earth and its atmosphere doing in this frame?

__(b)__ The muon lives $$0.000002\;\mathrm{s}$$ in its own frame. About how far does the ground travel toward the muon during the muon's life, given that it approaches at nearly the speed of light?

__(c)__ We now seem to have a paradox: (1) the muon is created $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the ground, (2) the muon lives only long enough for the ground to move about $$600\;\mathrm{m}$$ toward it, and yet (3) the ground reaches the muon before the muon decays. Explain why time dilation does __not__ resolve the paradox in this frame.

__(d)__ The two distances in statements (1) and (2) are measured in different reference frames: $$10{,}000\;\mathrm{m}$$ in the ground frame, but $$600\;\mathrm{m}$$ in the muon frame. Use this observation to resolve the paradox. In which frame must the height of the atmosphere be smaller, and roughly how small must it be?

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: Measuring a Moving Spaceship with a Stopwatch — Lizzie and Alex are in spaceships approaching each other with…
desc: Lizzie and Alex are in spaceships approaching each other with relative speed $$v.$$ Lizzie measures the length of her own ship, in her own reference frame, to be $$\ell_L.$$ Alex wants to measure the length of Lizzie's ship in __his__ frame, but all he has is a stopwatch and his…
statement:
Lizzie and Alex are in spaceships approaching each other with relative speed $$v.$$ Lizzie measures the length of her own ship, in her own reference frame, to be $$\ell_L.$$ Alex wants to measure the length of Lizzie's ship in __his__ frame, but all he has is a stopwatch and his knowledge of her speed $$v.$$ Recall from time dilation that a clock moving at speed $$v$$ runs slow by the factor $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$

__(a)__ Alex can only directly measure events that occur right where he is standing. Describe a measuring procedure using two events — $$F,$$ "the front of Lizzie's ship reaches Alex," and $$B,$$ "the back of Lizzie's ship reaches Alex" — that lets Alex compute the length $$\ell_A$$ of Lizzie's ship in his frame from the time $$t_A$$ on his stopwatch.

__(b)__ Events $$F$$ and $$B$$ also occur in Lizzie's frame. How far apart in space are they in her frame, and how much time $$t_L$$ passes between them in her frame?

__(c)__ Use time dilation to find the time $$t_A$$ that elapses on Alex's stopwatch between events $$F$$ and $$B,$$ in terms of $$\ell_L,$$ $$\gamma,$$ and $$v.$$

__(d)__ Combine your answers to find $$\ell_A$$ in terms of $$\ell_L$$ and $$\gamma.$$ Is Lizzie's ship longer or shorter in Alex's frame than in her own?

__(e)__ Is this result merely an optical trick — would a more careful measurement by Alex show the ship at its normal length? An object's length in its own rest frame is called its __proper length__. In Alex's frame, Lizzie herself is flattened along her direction of motion like a cardboard cutout. Is her health in danger from having her organs squeezed?

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: Grogg's One-Year Stopwatch, Solved with Length Contraction — Lizzie and Alex are at rest with respect to each…
desc: Lizzie and Alex are at rest with respect to each other, one light-year apart in outer space. Grogg drifts past Alex in his spaceship, heading straight toward Lizzie, and starts a stopwatch just as he passes Alex. Just as Grogg reaches Lizzie, his stopwatch reads exactly one…
statement:
Lizzie and Alex are at rest with respect to each other, one light-year apart in outer space. Grogg drifts past Alex in his spaceship, heading straight toward Lizzie, and starts a stopwatch just as he passes Alex. Just as Grogg reaches Lizzie, his stopwatch reads exactly one year. How fast do Alex and Lizzie measure Grogg to be going?

Solve the problem entirely in __Grogg's__ reference frame, where his stopwatch is at rest, using length contraction. (Use $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}},$$ and recall that a moving object is contracted along its motion by the factor $$\gamma.$$)

__(a)__ In Grogg's frame, Grogg is stationary while Alex and Lizzie drift past him at speed $$v.$$ How far apart are Alex and Lizzie in this frame?

__(b)__ Write an expression for the time $$t_G,$$ in Grogg's frame, between the event "Grogg passes Alex" and the event "Grogg passes Lizzie."

__(c)__ The problem tells you the value of $$t_G.$$ Set your expression equal to it and solve for $$v.$$

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: No Length Contraction Sideways — Length contraction shortens a moving object along its direction of motion by…
desc: Length contraction shortens a moving object along its direction of motion by the factor $$\gamma.$$ The directions perpendicular to the motion are called the __transverse__ directions. In this problem you will show that there is __no__ length contraction in the transverse…
statement:
Length contraction shortens a moving object along its direction of motion by the factor $$\gamma.$$ The directions perpendicular to the motion are called the __transverse__ directions. In this problem you will show that there is __no__ length contraction in the transverse directions.

__(a)__ A ball is a perfect sphere in its own rest frame. In our frame it moves to the right at relativistic speed $$v.$$ Assuming length contraction acts only along the direction of motion, what is the shape of the ball in our frame? How would the shape differ if length contraction also acted transversely by the same factor?

__(b)__ Time dilation was derived (last lesson) using a __light clock__: a light flash bouncing between two mirrors separated by a fixed distance __perpendicular__ to the clock's motion, with that mirror separation assumed to be the same in both frames. If transverse length contraction existed, what would happen to that derivation — and to everything built on it, including the derivation of length contraction itself?

__(c)__ Now for the decisive thought experiment. Two identical hollow cylinders, $$A$$ on the left and $$B$$ on the right, float in deep space facing each other, each with a paintbrush mounted on its outside surface. Cylinder $$A$$ moves to the right toward $$B.$$ Suppose (for contradiction) that moving objects contracted in __all__ directions. Working in $$B$$'s frame, what would happen when the cylinders meet?

__(d)__ Analyze the same encounter from $$A$$'s frame. Explain why the two analyses contradict each other, and why this contradiction with the principle of relativity proves that transverse length contraction cannot occur.

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: Synchronized Clocks and the Rear Clock Ahead Rule — Lizzie and Alex sit at opposite ends of a spaceship of…
desc: Lizzie and Alex sit at opposite ends of a spaceship of proper length $$\ell$$ — Alex at the left end, Lizzie at the right end. They want to clap their hands simultaneously, so they agree to clap at exactly noon as shown on their own clocks. Their clocks tick at the same rate…
statement:
Lizzie and Alex sit at opposite ends of a spaceship of proper length $$\ell$$ — Alex at the left end, Lizzie at the right end. They want to clap their hands simultaneously, so they agree to clap at exactly noon as shown on their own clocks. Their clocks tick at the same rate, but they worry that one clock might be set ahead of the other. To check, they install a lamp at the exact center of the ship that emits two light pulses at the same instant — one toward Alex, one toward Lizzie. Each finds that their clock strikes noon exactly as their light pulse arrives.

__(a)__ Explain why this test establishes that the two clocks are __synchronized__ in the ship's frame, so Alex and Lizzie will clap simultaneously in that frame.

__(b)__ Just as the light pulses leave the lamp, Grogg drifts by outside the ship, moving to the right at speed $$v$$ in the ship's frame. In Grogg's frame, the ship moves left at $$v$$ while both light pulses still travel at speed $$c$$ (the speed of light is invariant). Whose pulse arrives first in Grogg's frame? Whose clock therefore reaches noon first in Grogg's frame, and why must the event "Lizzie's clock reads noon as her pulse arrives" happen in every frame?

__(c)__ In Grogg's frame, the ship is length-contracted, so Lizzie and Alex are each a distance $$\dfrac{\ell}{2\gamma}$$ from the lamp. In this frame the gap between Lizzie and her (oncoming) pulse closes at the rate $$c + v,$$ while the gap between Alex and his pulse closes at only $$c - v.$$ Write expressions for the arrival times $$t_{L}$$ and $$t_{A}$$ of the two pulses in Grogg's frame, and show that the difference is $$\Delta t = t_A - t_L = \dfrac{\ell v \gamma}{c^2}.$$

__(d)__ In Grogg's frame, Lizzie's clock strikes noon a time $$\Delta t$$ before Alex's does — but the moving clocks also run slow by the factor $$\gamma.$$ By how much is Lizzie's clock __reading__ ahead of Alex's in Grogg's frame?

__(e)__ In Grogg's frame the ship moves left, so Alex is at the front of the ship and Lizzie is at the rear. State the general rule ("rear clock ahead") that summarizes this result. In Grogg's frame, does Lizzie's clock also __run faster__ than Alex's, or just stay ahead by a fixed amount?

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: A Row of Moving Clocks — A long row of identical clocks floats in space, all at rest with respect to each…
desc: A long row of identical clocks floats in space, all at rest with respect to each other and synchronized in their shared rest frame. Alex flies past the row to the right at speed $$v.$$ In the clock frame, at the moment Alex reaches the leftmost clock, every clock reads zero. Let…
statement:
A long row of identical clocks floats in space, all at rest with respect to each other and synchronized in their shared rest frame. Alex flies past the row to the right at speed $$v.$$ In the clock frame, at the moment Alex reaches the leftmost clock, every clock reads zero. Let the distance from the first (leftmost) clock to the last (rightmost) clock be $$\ell$$ in the clock frame. Use $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$$ and the rear-clock-ahead rule: clocks synchronized in their own frame and separated by proper distance $$d$$ along their motion appear, in a frame where they move at $$v,$$ with the rear clock ahead by $$\dfrac{v d}{c^2}.$$

__(a)__ Describe how the picture above transforms into Alex's frame, drawn at the event where the first clock reaches him. What happens to Alex's ship, to the clocks' velocities, to the spacing between the clocks, and to the readings shown on the clocks?

__(b)__ Working in the clock frame, find the reading on the __last__ clock at the event where Alex reaches it.

__(c)__ Now redo the calculation in Alex's frame. How far must the last clock travel to reach Alex, and how long does that take in his frame? Given that moving clocks run slow by $$\gamma,$$ how much does the last clock __advance__ during the trip? Combining that with the last clock's reading at the start (from the rear-clock-ahead rule), show that the last clock reads $$\dfrac{\ell}{v}$$ when it reaches Alex.

__(d)__ Why is it essential that the two calculations agree?

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: The Ship in the Barn — Lizzie's spaceship has proper length $$10\;\mathrm{m}.$$ She approaches a tunnel of…
desc: Lizzie's spaceship has proper length $$10\;\mathrm{m}.$$ She approaches a tunnel of proper length $$6\;\mathrm{m}$$ fast enough that her Lorentz factor in the tunnel's frame is $$\gamma = 2$$ (so $$v \approx 0.866\,c$$). __(a)__ The picture above is drawn in the tunnel's frame…
statement:
Lizzie's spaceship has proper length $$10\;\mathrm{m}.$$ She approaches a tunnel of proper length $$6\;\mathrm{m}$$ fast enough that her Lorentz factor in the tunnel's frame is $$\gamma = 2$$ (so $$v \approx 0.866\,c$$).

__(a)__ The picture above is drawn in the tunnel's frame. Why is Lizzie's ship drawn only $$5\;\mathrm{m}$$ long? In this frame, does her ship ever fit entirely inside the tunnel? Now answer the same question in Lizzie's frame: how long is the tunnel there, and does her ship fit?

__(b)__ Is "the ship is completely inside the tunnel" a single event? Break the claim down into two events — one involving the front of the ship and one involving the back — and explain how the relativity of simultaneity dissolves the apparent contradiction between the two frames.

__(c)__ To sharpen the paradox, replace the tunnel with an indestructible, immovable __barn__ of the same $$6\;\mathrm{m}$$ proper length, with a door that slams shut at the event where the back of Lizzie's ship passes inside. When the front of her ship hits the barn's back wall, the front stops (in the barn frame). Also imagine Alex drifting alongside Lizzie at her speed (slightly higher up, so he misses the barn) — he stays inertial the whole time. Simplicio argues: "In Alex's frame the barn is only $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ long. When the ship's front hits the wall, the ship stops with most of it still sticking out, the back never enters, and the door never closes — but in the barn frame the door does close. Contradiction!" Simplicio assumes the whole ship stops at once in Alex's frame. Why is that impossible? (Think about how fast the news "the front has stopped" can possibly travel down the ship — and what that says about perfectly rigid objects.)

__(d)__ Assume the "news" travels backward through the ship as a shock wave moving at the speed of light $$c.$$ Define event (1): the front of the ship hits the back wall and stops; event (2): the shock wave reaches the back of the ship, which then stops. Work in the __barn frame__: at event (1) the back of the (still $$5\;\mathrm{m}$$-long, still moving) ship is $$5\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the shock wave. The back of the ship moves at $$0.866\,c$$ while the shock wave approaches it at $$c.$$ If the back of the ship moves a distance $$x$$ and the shock wave moves a distance $$d$$ between events (1) and (2), then $$x + d = 5\;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$x = 0.866\,d.$$ Find the final length of the (telescopingly crumpled) ship in the barn frame. Does the ship end up inside the barn, and does the door close?

__(e)__ Repeat in __Alex's frame__, where the ship is initially $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ long and at rest, and the barn (length $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ here) rushes at it at $$0.866\,c.$$ After event (1), the barn's back wall pushes the ship's front along at $$0.866\,c$$ while the shock wave travels backward through the ship at $$c.$$ The shock wave must cover the full $$10\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Find the ship's final length in Alex's frame, and check whether the ship fits in the barn in this frame too.

__(f)__ The final lengths in parts (d) and (e) disagree. Is that a contradiction? To check consistency, imagine the barn divided lengthwise into ten equal slats, numbered 1 to 10 starting from the entrance. In the barn frame, the crumpled ship's front touches the far wall, so event (2) — the shock wave reaching the back of the ship — happens $$6\;\mathrm{m} - 2.68\;\mathrm{m} = 3.32\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the entrance. Which slat is that? Now locate event (2) in Alex's frame ($$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ barn, final ship length $$1.34\;\mathrm{m}$$) and show it lands on the same slat.

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: The Cookie Cutter Paradox — In a (fancifully relativistic) cookie factory, a sheet of cookie dough rides a…
desc: In a (fancifully relativistic) cookie factory, a sheet of cookie dough rides a conveyor belt moving at speed $$v,$$ a substantial fraction of the speed of light. A cookie cutter shaped like an equilateral triangle, with horizontal width $$\ell$$ in the factory frame, is brought…
statement:
In a (fancifully relativistic) cookie factory, a sheet of cookie dough rides a conveyor belt moving at speed $$v,$$ a substantial fraction of the speed of light. A cookie cutter shaped like an equilateral triangle, with horizontal width $$\ell$$ in the factory frame, is brought straight down onto the dough; in the __factory frame__, every part of the cutter strikes the dough simultaneously. After being cut, the cookies ride off the belt and are sold in a store, where they are at rest; assume each cookie keeps the shape it had in its own rest frame while on the belt. The Lorentz factor of the belt is $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}.$$

__(a)__ In the factory frame, the cookies on the belt are equilateral triangles. Three candidate shapes for the cookies you buy in the store are shown below: (A) stretched horizontally, (B) squashed horizontally, (C) equilateral. Which is correct, and why? (Horizontal means along the belt's motion.)

__(b)__ Here is an argument for the opposite answer: "In the dough's rest frame, the cutter is the moving object, so the cutter is length-contracted to width $$\ell/\gamma.$$ A skinny cutter cuts skinny cookies, so the cookies are squashed." The cookies cannot be both stretched and squashed. What relativistic effect does this argument overlook?

__(c)__ Let event $$R$$ be "the right edge of the cutter touches the dough" and event $$L$$ be "the left edge of the cutter touches the dough." Imagine clocks mounted on the two edges of the cutter, synchronized in the cutter's frame and reading zero at events $$R$$ and $$L$$ respectively. In the dough frame, the cutter moves to the __left__ at speed $$v.$$ Use the rear-clock-ahead rule — for clocks of proper separation $$\ell$$ moving at speed $$v,$$ the rear clock reads ahead by $$\dfrac{v\ell}{c^2}$$ — to decide which edge of the cutter touches the dough first in the dough frame.

__(d)__ Make the dough-frame analysis quantitative. In the dough frame, how much time passes between events $$R$$ and $$L$$? (Remember the cutter's clocks run slow by $$\gamma$$ in this frame.) How far does the cutter move leftward during that time? Adding the cutter's contracted width $$\ell/\gamma,$$ show that the width of the cookie cut from the dough is $$w = \dfrac{\gamma v^2 \ell}{c^2} + \dfrac{\ell}{\gamma} = \gamma\ell,$$ and explain how the factory-frame analysis makes the answer $$\gamma \ell$$ obvious without any algebra.

__(e)__ In the factory frame the descending cutter is level (horizontal). What is different about the cutter's orientation in the dough frame that makes it possible for one edge to strike before the other?

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: Bell's Spaceship Paradox — This scenario is named after J.S. Bell, the physicist who popularized it. Alex and…
desc: This scenario is named after J.S. Bell, the physicist who popularized it. Alex and Lizzie sit in identical spaceships, initially at rest in Grogg's frame, with Lizzie directly ahead of (to the right of) Alex. A weak rope with a little slack connects the two ships…
statement:
This scenario is named after J.S. Bell, the physicist who popularized it. Alex and Lizzie sit in identical spaceships, initially at rest in Grogg's frame, with Lizzie directly ahead of (to the right of) Alex. A weak rope with a little slack connects the two ships. Simultaneously, as seen in Grogg's frame, both pilots fire their engines and accelerate to the right, always maintaining exactly the same acceleration as each other in Grogg's frame, getting faster and faster. Does the rope ever break?

__(a)__ In Grogg's frame, what happens to the distance between the two ships as they speed up? What happens to the rope itself as it moves faster and faster in Grogg's frame, and what do these two facts together imply?

__(b)__ Alex offers a counterargument: "Lizzie and I fire our engines simultaneously and accelerate identically, so she always matches my velocity and stays the same distance ahead of me. In my frame the rope is not length-contracted, so it never breaks." One immediate objection is that Alex is in an accelerating, non-inertial frame. To sidestep that objection, modify the problem: instead of firing engines continuously, Alex shoots a pellet out the back of his ship (instantly boosting his speed), then coasts for ten seconds of his own time, fires another pellet, and so on. Lizzie follows exactly the same protocol, starting simultaneously with Alex in Grogg's frame. In __Grogg's__ frame, do Alex and Lizzie fire each of their pellets simultaneously?

__(c)__ Alex and Lizzie agree they fired their __first__ pellets simultaneously (before it, they shared Grogg's frame). After the first pellet, they coast in a new shared inertial frame, moving to the right, carrying clocks that are synchronized with each other in that new frame. Using the rear-clock-ahead rule (rear clock ahead by $$\dfrac{v\ell}{c^2}$$ in a frame where the clocks move at $$v$$ with proper separation $$\ell$$), determine: in their new frame, who fires the __second__ pellet first?

__(d)__ So does the rope break, analyzed in Alex and Lizzie's own frames? Reconcile this with Alex's original argument, and state the conclusion of the paradox.

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: The Twin Paradox — Alex and Lizzie are both 12 years old. Lizzie boards a spaceship and travels to the right…
desc: Alex and Lizzie are both 12 years old. Lizzie boards a spaceship and travels to the right at $$v \approx 0.995\,c,$$ so that $$\gamma = 10,$$ for 40 years as measured in Alex's frame. Then she turns around (very quickly) and travels back at the same speed for another 40 years in…
statement:
Alex and Lizzie are both 12 years old. Lizzie boards a spaceship and travels to the right at $$v \approx 0.995\,c,$$ so that $$\gamma = 10,$$ for 40 years as measured in Alex's frame. Then she turns around (very quickly) and travels back at the same speed for another 40 years in Alex's frame, arriving for a reunion. Alex stays home in an inertial frame the whole time.

__(a)__ Define event 1: Lizzie departs; event 2: Lizzie turns around; event 3: the reunion. Explain why each twin's age __at event 3__ is an invariant (the same in every frame). Then find both ages at the reunion: how old is Alex, and how old is Lizzie?

__(b)__ Here is the paradox. From Lizzie's perspective, Alex is the one who rushes away and comes back at $$0.995\,c,$$ so __his__ clock runs slow by $$\gamma = 10$$ for almost her whole trip. Since Lizzie ages 8 years, this reasoning predicts Alex ages only $$0.8$$ years and is $$12.8$$ at the reunion — contradicting part (a). What is wrong with applying this symmetric reasoning to Lizzie?

__(c)__ To analyze the turnaround cleanly with only inertial frames, introduce Grogg (whose ship travels outbound at $$0.995\,c$$ in Alex's frame, carrying Lizzie on the first leg) and Winnie (whose ship travels inbound at $$0.995\,c$$; Lizzie jumps aboard at event 2). Give Alex two clocks that always show his age in his frame: "Alex's Clock," kept with Alex, and the "Turnaround Clock," placed at the turnaround point, synchronized with Alex's Clock in his frame. In Alex's frame the turnaround point is $$\ell \approx 39.8$$ light-years away ($$40\;\mathrm{yr} \times 0.995\,c$$). What do Alex's Clock and the Turnaround Clock read at the time of event 2 in __Alex's__ frame? Which reading is invariant, and why?

__(d)__ Now fill in the rest of this chart, which lists what each clock reads simultaneously with event 2, as judged in each frame: $$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Viewer} & \text{Alex's Clock (yr)} & \text{Turnaround Clock (yr)} \\ \hline \text{Alex} & 52 & 52 \\ \text{Grogg (Lizzie outbound)} & \text{(i)} & 52 \\ \text{Winnie (Lizzie inbound)} & \text{(ii)} & 52 \end{array}$$ For (i), use time dilation: in Grogg's frame, only 4 years pass between events 1 and 2. Check your answer against the rear-clock-ahead rule, $$\dfrac{v\ell}{c^2} \approx \dfrac{0.995\,c \times 39.8\;\mathrm{ly}}{c^2} \approx 39.6\;\mathrm{yr}.$$ For (ii), note that in Winnie's frame the clocks move in the opposite direction, so the other clock is the rear clock.

__(e)__ Use the chart to resolve the paradox: what happens to "Alex's age right now," according to Lizzie, at the moment she jumps from Grogg's ship to Winnie's?

lesson: REL02: Length Contraction, Simultaneity, and Paradoxes
label: REL02
name: Making Sense of the Velocity Addition Formula — In Galilean (everyday) relativity, velocities simply add: if…
desc: In Galilean (everyday) relativity, velocities simply add: if Lizzie moves right at $$5\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in Alex's frame and Grogg moves left at $$3\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in Alex's frame, then Grogg approaches Lizzie at $$8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in her frame. But simple addition cannot be…
statement:
In Galilean (everyday) relativity, velocities simply add: if Lizzie moves right at $$5\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in Alex's frame and Grogg moves left at $$3\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in Alex's frame, then Grogg approaches Lizzie at $$8\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in her frame. But simple addition cannot be exactly right in special relativity — applied to a light flash it would make the speed of light differ between frames, violating Einstein's postulate. A careful analysis (tracking a row of synchronized clocks in Alex's frame, then applying length contraction, time dilation, and rear-clock-ahead in Lizzie's frame) yields the exact rule. If Lizzie moves at speed $$v$$ (toward Alex from one side) and Grogg at speed $$u$$ (toward Alex from the other side), both measured in Alex's frame, then Grogg's speed in __Lizzie's__ frame is the __velocity addition formula__: $$u_L = \dfrac{u + v}{1 + \dfrac{uv}{c^2}}.$$

__(a)__ For the everyday case $$v = 5\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and $$u = 3\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ explain — without a calculator — why the formula gives almost exactly $$8\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and whether the exact answer is slightly faster or slightly slower. (In fact it works out to $$7.999999999999998\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$) What does this say about why Galilean relativity works so well in daily life?

__(b)__ Check the case $$v = 0.$$ What does the formula give, and why does that make sense?

__(c)__ Check the case $$u = c$$ (replace Grogg with a flash of light). What does the formula give, and which postulate of relativity does this confirm?

__(d)__ Compute $$u_L$$ for $$u = v = 0.8\,c.$$ What is the most important feature of the result?

__(e)__ The formula has the property that increasing either $$u$$ or $$v$$ increases $$u_L.$$ Use this, together with part (c), to argue that adding any two speeds less than $$c$$ always yields a speed less than $$c.$$ What does this imply about a rocket that repeatedly fires its engine in bursts, gaining the same boost (as measured in its own momentary rest frame) with each burst — can it ever reach the speed of light?
